paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Buckville, Arkansas, was a 1919 night-rider campaign in which a white band dynamited, burned and shot up the homes of a Black farming settlement about 20 miles northwest of Hot Springs. The main raid, dated to March 29, reportedly left only a Baptist minister's home standing, and the local prosecutor was quoted as saying every Black family had been driven out. In June grand jury indictments led to the arrest of six white men, two sets of brothers, on arson charges. Black newspapers presented the attack as a land grab by prominent whites and linked the accused to a newly organized Ku Klux Klan.

Black residents owned farm land around the village that the Chicago Defender described as the choicest in the Ouachita valley. According to the Defender, whites had repeatedly offered to buy these lands, and the owners had always declined. The Hot Springs Echo wrote that the night riders sought to "secure possession of the fertile farm lands owned by the Negro contingent."

The Black papers dated the main raid to March 29, when a group of men entered the village of Buckville, dynamited houses, poured kerosene on churches and set the town ablaze. As residents ran from the burning dwellings, shots were fired at them. The Echo described weeks of terror in which homes were shot up and dynamite "freely used," and it claimed a murder had been committed, though it named no one killed.

Among those who suffered, the Echo listed Sue Bledsoe, Jeff Kelly and Jinsy Hill, and it said the house of Jeff Hollis was "blown off the face of the earth by dynamite." The Defender's account named the houses of Mrs. Susie Bledsoe, Jefferson Kelly and Jon Hollis and said one planter escaped before the night riders could fire on him. The only residence left standing, according to the Defender, belonged to a Baptist minister, whom the Echo called Doss Haily.

The Echo reported in early May that the Garland County sheriff had gone to the scene to make arrests. On June 7 the Defender said six prominent white men were suspected, but the authorities had withheld their names. Six indictments had been drawn after witnesses went before a grand jury.

A Hot Springs dispatch of June 20 reported the arrest of Virgil, Frank and Samuel Housely and Green, Porter and William Brown, jailed awaiting trial on arson charges. The Brown brothers were accused of furnishing the dynamite. No report of a trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

The Hot Springs Echo, a Black paper in the nearest city, carried the earliest report found, on May 3, describing a "reign of terror" by a "Night Riding gang" of "some of the most prominent white men" in the Buckville section. National coverage followed a month later, when the Chicago Defender ran a Century News Service dispatch on its front page of June 7 under the headline "Ku Klux Ride in Arkansas." Its subheads "Prominent Men Involved" and "Whites Want Land" framed the attack as a scheme to force Black landowners "to sell out and leave," and the text said the settlement had been "literally wiped from the earth" by dynamite.

On June 21 the Defender reported the arrests under the headline "Nab Night Riders Who Burned Many Homes," and the same Hot Springs dispatch ran in the Colorado Statesman on June 28 among a front-page column of race news briefs. Both versions stressed the reported Klan tie and its aim of preventing Black citizens "from exercising their right of suffrage."

The reports differ on the county: the Echo said the Garland County sheriff went to make arrests, while the Defender tied the suspects to families in Hot Spring County in one copy and Hot Springs in another. The scale differs as well, since the June 20 dispatch tied the indictments to the burning of the homes of "three prominent families," while the Echo quoted Prosecutor Hoskins as saying every Black family had been driven out. Only the Echo alleged a killing, and none of the reports names anyone who died.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Buckville, Arkansas
bases: A night-riding band dynamited, burned and shot up the homes of a Black landowning settlement to force its residents to sell and leave, and the prosecutor was quoted as saying every Black family had been driven out (A1, A2, A5, A8).

The local Hot Springs Echo (A1, A2), a Century News Service dispatch in the Chicago Defender (A3-A5) and a later Hot Springs dispatch on the arrests (A6, A8) independently agree on a dynamite-and-arson night-rider attack on Black homes near Buckville.

accounts.gist: A night-riding gang of prominent white men waged weeks of terror to seize Black-owned farm land, shooting up homes, using dynamite and committing a murder; the prosecutor said every Black family was driven out.

accounts.label: Century News Service dispatch
accounts.gist: Night riders with dynamite wiped out the Black settlement about March 29; six prominent white men were suspected and indicted, their names withheld, the motive being the land.

accounts.label: Hot Springs dispatch on the arrests
accounts.gist: Six brothers from two families, said to include Klan members, were jailed on arson charges for dynamiting houses, burning churches and firing on fleeing residents on March 29.

framing.detail: The Hot Springs Echo called it a 'reign of terror' by a 'Night Riding gang' of prominent whites seeking Black-owned farm land.
The Chicago Defender headlined 'Ku Klux Ride in Arkansas' with subheads 'Prominent Men Involved' and 'Whites Want Land', and said the settlement was 'wiped from the earth'.
'Nab Night Riders Who Burned Many Homes' (Defender) and the Colorado Statesman's copy stressed the Klan's aim of keeping the Race from voting.
